title: Gastric Decompression via NG Tube
description: Students assess abdominal symptoms, insert an NG tube for decompression, manage ongoing suction, educate the patient, and document results.
learningObjective:
Perform a focused assessment of an adult with abdominal distention, discomfort, and nausea/vomiting. 
Safely insert and manage a nasogastric tube and initiate gastric decompression. 
Provide patient education and support related to a temporary NG tube for gastric decompression. 
Document key findings and results of assessments and interventions.

actions.title: Adjust Bed to Working Height
actions.prompt: Indicate the most appropriate height you adjust the bed to when at the bedside assessing the patient, performing interventions, or assisting the patient in bed.
items: Raise the bed to the maximum available height, keep all side rails down to make it easier to reach the patient and lean over the patient as necessary.
Leave the bed at the current height, stand with feet close together for balance, and lean forward with straight legs.
Lower the bed completely to keep the patient safe and sit on the bed or bend at the waist as necessary to provide care or assess the patient.
Raise the bed to a comfortable working height for yourself and stand close to the patient with knees slightly bent.
actions.correct: Raise the bed to a comfortable working height for yourself and stand close to the patient with knees slightly bent.
actions.resultName: The bed height has been adjusted to a comfortable working height for use of safe body mechanics.

actions.title: Confirm NPO Status with Patient
actions.prompt: Before preparing for NG tube insertion, which statement by the nurse best demonstrates correct verification of the patient’s NPO status?
items: “Have you eaten or had anything to drink, including water, gum, or hard candy, while you have been admitted to the hospital?”
“I see an NPO order in your chart, so I’ll assume you haven’t had anything to eat or drink today.”
“You haven’t been given a meal tray, so I know you’ve been NPO.”
“Your nausea has been pretty bad, so I’m sure you haven’t tried to drink anything.”
actions.correct: “Have you eaten or had anything to drink, including water, gum, or hard candy, while you have been admitted to the hospital?”
actions.resultName: Patient will confirm when she last had oral when asked (food, fluids, gum, ice chips, or medications).

actions.title: Gather and Prepare Supplies and Equipment
actions.prompt: The nurse is preparing to insert an NG tube for gastric decompression. Which of the following sets of supplies and equipment reflects correct and complete preparation before beginning the procedure?
items: NG tube, sterile gloves, suction canister, petroleum-based lubricant, sterile field drape, and emesis basin.
NG tube, alcohol-based hand sanitizer, ice chips for comfort, oral medications for nausea, and suction tubing connected directly to the wall without a canister.
NG tube, water‑soluble lubricant, clean gloves, tape or securement device, cup of water with straw, emesis basin, and functioning suction setup (canister, regulator, tubing).
NG tube, water bottle for patient hydration, oral thermometer, clean gloves, large syringe for IV use, and non‑rebreather mask.
actions.correct: NG tube, water‑soluble lubricant, clean gloves, tape or securement device, cup of water with straw, emesis basin, and functioning suction setup (canister, regulator, tubing).
actions.resultName: All required supplies for NG tube insertion have been gathered

actions.title: Monitor Intake & Output
actions.prompt: A nurse has just connected a patient’s newly inserted NG tube to low‑intermittent suction. Which action demonstrates correct monitoring of the NG tube output?
items: Document only the total volume at the end of the shift because early measurements are unnecessary.
Clamp the NG tube every hour to check whether the patient still feels nauseated before recording output.
Assess the color, consistency, and amount of output; ensure the suction is functioning; and record the initial drainage volume as soon as suction begins.
Increase suction pressure if output is minimal during the first 5 minutes.
actions.correct: Assess the color, consistency, and amount of output; ensure the suction is functioning; and record the initial drainage volume as soon as suction begins.
actions.resultName: NG tube connected to low‑intermittent suction per provider order. Initial output measured at 150 mL green, watery gastric fluid collected in suction canister within the first 20 minutes.

actions.title: Perform Focused Gastrointestinal Assessment - Initial
actions.prompt: Indicate what you would assess as part of an initial focused gastrointestinal assessment on this patient.

concepts.description: Inspection (shape, symmetry, distention, scars, visible peristalsis), Auscultation (all 4 quadrants; frequency, character), Palpation (light then deep; tenderness, guarding, rebound)
Last bowel movement & stool characteristics, Nausea/vomiting pattern, oral intake tolerance
Pain assessment (quality, region, pattern), Hydration status (mucous membranes)

actions.resultName: Abdomen visibly distended and taut; hypoactive bowel sounds x4 quadrants; mild diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs; multiple episodes of non‑bloody vomiting; unable to tolerate even sips of water; mucous membranes mildly dry

actions.title: Perform Focused Gastrointestinal Assessment - Reassessment

Assess NG tube site and functioning

actions.resultName: Abdomen still distended but less tense; decreased nausea (“feels better”); ~150 mL green gastric fluid output (during initial 15-20 minutes post insertion of NG tube); bowel sounds remain hypoactive; skin around nares mildly irritated

actions.resultName: Respiratory status is stable and assessment is within normal limits.

actions.title: Perform Focused Respiratory Assessment - Reassessment
actions.prompt: Indicate what you would assess as part of a focused respiratory re-assessment on this patient.

concepts.description: Reassess respiratory rate and work of breathing after nasogastric tube placed
Check for improvement in discomfort‑related tachypnea
Confirm head of bed elevation for aspiration risk reduction

actions.resultName: Respiratory status is stable and assessment is within normal limits; breath sounds still clear; no distress noted; SpO₂ stable; patient breathing easier now that abdominal pressure is reduced

actions.title: Perform Nasogastric Tube Clamping
actions.prompt: A student nurse clamps the NG tube of a patient receiving gastric decompression to “let the stomach rest.” Which of the following statements reflects the correct understanding of why this action is inappropriate in this clinical situation?
items: Clamping the NG tube prevents air from entering the stomach but does not affect fluid removal.
Clamping the NG tube during gastric decompression can worsen abdominal distention, increase nausea and vomiting, and raise aspiration risk.
Clamping the NG tube prevents air from entering the stomach but does not affect fluid removal.
Clamping the NG tube is required whenever the patient asks for a break from suction.
actions.correct: Clamping the NG tube during gastric decompression can worsen abdominal distention, increase nausea and vomiting, and raise aspiration risk.
actions.resultName: Abdomen noted to be distended with mild increase in discomfort.

actions.title: Perform Nasogastric Tube Insertion
actions.prompt: Arrange the following steps in chronological order for how they should be performed to demonstrate adherence to best-practice guidelines during insertion of a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression.
items: Assess patient readiness and nasal patency and drape patient with towel or chux
Measure tube length (from tip of nose to earlobe to halfway between xiphoid process and umbilicus) and mark tube length with tape or marker
Lubricate distal 2-4 inches of NG tube with water-soluble lubricant and insert NG tube into selected nostril
Advance NG tube into nasopharynx and ask/assist patient to tuck chin to chest and swallow repeatedly, then advance tube with each swallow
Advance tube to pre-measured length and secure tube at nostril
actions.resultName: NG tube inserted. Patient experienced brief gagging but remained able to speak and breathe without difficulty. Respirations unlabored; SpO₂ 98% RA. No complications observed.

actions.title: Perform Nasogastric Tube Placement Check
actions.prompt: After inserting a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression, which action by the nurse best reflects evidence‑based practice for verifying NG‑tube placement at the bedside prior to connecting to suction?
items: Checking for a “gurgling” sound over the epigastric area while instilling air through the tube.
Assessing for patient coughing or respiratory distress during insertion, as this confirms gastric placement.
Asking the patient to speak while the tube is in place, as the ability to talk proves that the tube is in the stomach.
Aspirating gastric contents and evaluating the color and pH, while ensuring the external length of tubing matches the measured insertion depth.
actions.correct: Aspirating gastric contents and evaluating the color and pH, while ensuring the external length of tubing matches the measured insertion depth.
actions.resultName: Placement was verified using gastric aspirate evaluation. Aspirated green, watery gastric fluid; pH measured at 3, consistent with gastric placement. External tube marking at nare remained at premeasured length, matching measured insertion depth. No coughing, respiratory distress, or difficulty speaking observed during or after verification.

actions.title: Perform Nasogastric Tube Removal
actions.prompt: Arrange the following steps in chronological order for how they should be performed to demonstrate adherence to best-practice guidelines during removal of a nasogastric tube currently in place for gastric decompression.
items: Turn off suction, disconnect tubing from suction system, then clamp or kink tube to prevent spillage
Remove securement device from nose and instruct patient to take three deep breaths in and out
Remove the tube swiftly and smoothing during exhalation
Place tube into disposable bag and clean or assist with cleaning nares, face, oral cavity
actions.resultName: Nasogastric tube removed from patient.

actions.title: Provide Patient Education - General
actions.prompt: When teaching a patient about their plan of care during an acute episode of abdominal distention and nausea, which of the following communication strategies best supports patient understanding and reduces anxiety?
items: Explain procedures using short chunks of information and pause frequently to check for understanding.
Provide all necessary education at the beginning of the encounter so the patient hears the “full plan” up front.
Wait until the patient asks questions to avoid overwhelming them with details they may not want.
Avoid repeating information unless the patient appears confused.
actions.correct: Explain procedures using short chunks of information and pause frequently to check for understanding.
actions.resultName: Patient nodded and appeared engaged in education.

actions.title: Provide Patient Education – Purpose of NG Tube
actions.prompt: A patient asks, “Why do I need this tube in my nose?” Which nurse response best explains the purpose of the NG tube in this scenario?
items: “The tube lets us give you medications more quickly.”
“The tube helps your stomach empty so the pressure, nausea, and vomiting can improve.”
“The tube helps us see if you need surgery later.”
“The tube will help your bowel movements return immediately.”
actions.correct: “The tube helps your stomach empty so the pressure, nausea, and vomiting can improve.”
actions.resultName: Patient nodded and appeared engaged in education.

actions.title: Provide Patient Education – NG Tube Insertion Procedure
actions.prompt: When preparing a patient for NG tube insertion, which explanation best prepares them for what to expect during the procedure?
items: “You shouldn’t feel anything at all—this is usually painless.”
“You will feel a strong burning sensation; this is normal and cannot be reduced.”
“Most patients vomit during insertion, but that means the tube is in the right place.”
“You may gag or have watery eyes, but I’ll guide you to take slow breaths and swallow to make it easier.”
actions.correct: “You may gag or have watery eyes, but I’ll guide you to take slow breaths and swallow to make it easier.”
actions.resultName: Patient nodded and appeared engaged in education.

actions.title: Provide Patient Education – NG Tube Safety and Comfort
actions.prompt: Which teaching point is most important for maintaining patient safety after the NG tube has been inserted?
items: “If the tape comes loose, just push the tube back in yourself.”
“You may chew gum or eat ice chips at any time to keep your mouth moist.”
“You should lie flat after the tube is placed to help the suction work better.”
“Keep the head of your bed elevated to reduce your risk of vomiting or aspiration.”
actions.correct: “Keep the head of your bed elevated to reduce your risk of vomiting or aspiration.”
actions.resultName: Patient nodded and appeared engaged in education.

actions.title: Provide Patient Education – Suction for Gastric Decompression
actions.prompt: Which explanation accurately describes the suction connected to the patient’s NG tube?
items: “The suction pulls air and fluid out of your stomach to relieve the pressure that’s making you nauseated."
“The suction gives your stomach medication to help it empty.”
“The suction inflates your intestines so we can better assess them.”
“The suction is only for collecting samples; it won’t change your symptoms.”
actions.correct: “The suction pulls air and fluid out of your stomach to relieve the pressure that’s making you nauseated."
actions.resultName: Patient nodded and appeared engaged in education.

actions.title: Suction Initiation – Connecting to NG Tube
actions.prompt: Arrange the following items in chronological order for how they should be performed to adhere to best-practice guidelines for initiating suction on an NG tube.
items: Ensure NG tube placement has been verified and ensure suction canister is securely/appropriately mounted to wall bracket or stand before use
Connect vacuum tubing from wall suction port to canister “vac” or “in” port
Turn on wall suction to confirm suction system is functioning, then turn back off
Attach patient suction tubing to the NG tube connector snuggly
Turn on wall suction and adjust to ordered setting
Observe initial suction function by watching for movement of fluid/air in tubing
actions.resultName: Suction has been initiated. Initial output of thin green gastric fluid observed.

actions.title: Suction Set-Up – Preparing Suction Canister, Regulator, and Tubing
actions.prompt: While preparing to initiate gastric decompression for a patient with a newly placed NG tube, the nurse begins setting up wall suction. Which of the following steps demonstrates the correct sequence for preparing the suction canister, regulator, and tubing before attaching the NG tube?
items:
1) Connect patient tubing directly to the wall suction port
2) Turn the regulator to full suction
3) Attach the canister after suction is already running

1) Attach the suction canister to the wall bracket and connect the canister’s vacuum port to the wall suction source
2) Connect the patient tubing to the canister’s patient port
3) Adjust the suction regulator to the prescribed level

1) Attach patient tubing to the wall suction source
2) Leave the canister empty to prevent contamination
3) Set suction to continuous high suction

1) Fill the suction canister with sterile water
2) Attach the regulator to the patient tubing
3) Connect the tubing directly to the NG tube
actions.correct:
1) Attach the suction canister to the wall bracket and connect the canister’s vacuum port to the wall suction source
2) Connect the patient tubing to the canister’s patient port
3) Adjust the suction regulator to the prescribed level
actions.resultName: Suction has been set up.

communicationCriteria.title: Demonstrate empathy
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student demonstrated empathy. Look for acknowledging feelings, validating concerns, expressing care, and using reassuring language — not just clinical task completion. Return PASS only if there are clear empathic statements, FAIL if the encounter is purely transactional.

communicationCriteria.title: Use patient-centered, therapeutic communication strategies
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate for patient-centered communication using open-ended questions, allowing the patient to elaborate, summarizing back, checking for understanding, avoiding interruptions, and including the patient in decision-making. Also evaluate for the use of therapeutic communication techniques (active listening, empathy, reflection) to acknowledge the patient’s anxiety, discomfort, and concerns while promoting safety and trust. Return PASS if multiple patient-centered and therapeutic communication strategies are visible.

communicationCriteria.title: Use clear, health-literacy sensitive language
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student used clear, plain language and explained any medical terms (e.g., NPO, metabolic, hemorrhage) in patient-friendly words, as well as explained assessment findings and procedures in plain, health‑literacy–sensitive language. If the student used jargon without explanation or responded poorly when the patient said they did not understand, return FAIL. Return PASS only if education was accessible.

communicationCriteria.title: Establish rapport
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student established rapport with the patient at the start of the encounter using a calm, respectful, and non-judgmental tone. Did the student introduce themselves by name, confirm patient identity (name + DOB), use a warm tone, and orient the patient to what would happen? Return PASS only if most of these are present.

aiPatientData.specialPatientInfo:
I haven’t had anything to eat or drink since yesterday afternoon because I was told not to. My stomach feels very full and tight, and the nausea has been constant. I feel like I could throw up at any time. 

 

I feel nervous about having a tube placed through my nose because I think it might make me gag and feel uncomfortable in my throat, but I’m willing to go through it because I want the pressure and nausea to get better. 

 

After the tube is placed, the pressure in my stomach feels better and the nausea improves, but my nose and throat feel sore and irritated. I understand I need to keep my head up, not pull on the tube, and let someone know if my symptoms get worse.

sbar.situation:
The date and time of this simulated clinical encounter is: April 10th at 10:30. 

Sofia Delgado, 34-year-old female admitted this morning with abdominal distention, nausea, and several episodes of non-bloody vomiting over the last 56 hours. Provider has ordered NG tube insertion for gastric decompression.
sbar.background: History of intermittent constipation, no prior abdominal surgeries. Symptoms began yesterday evening and have progressively worsened. Last bowel movement was three days ago. No known food poisoning exposure. No pregnancy. Vital signs have been stable. No prior NG tube experience.
sbar.assessment: Patient is alert and anxious, guarding abdomen during movement. Abdomen appears distended with hypoactive bowel sounds in all quadrants. Reports ongoing nausea and a sensation of “pressure.” Denies fever. Maintaining hydration but tolerating very little oral intake. IV access already initiated with 0.9% NS running at 100 mL/hr.
sbar.recommendation: Insert an NG tube per provider order and begin gastric decompression. Monitor patient comfort, abdominal distention, and suction output. Provide reassurance and education throughout the procedure. Document assessment, interventions, and patient response.
